passages.happening:
Joseph tells Pharaoh that his family has arrived and is in Goshen (verse 1). He brings five of his brothers to meet him (verse 2).

“What is your occupation?” Pharaoh asks. “Your servants are shepherds,” they reply, “both we and our fathers” (verse 3). They ask to live in Egypt for a time, “because there is no pasture for the flocks of your servants” (verse 4).

Pharaoh says to Joseph, “the land of Egypt is before you; settle your father and brothers in the best part of the land. They may dwell in the land of Goshen” (verse 6). If any of them are skilled, they can take charge of Pharaoh's own livestock (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The brothers say exactly what Joseph told them to say (46:33-34). They are shepherds. They come as guests, ‘to live in the land for a time’. The Hebrew word means to stay as a foreigner, without owning land. They do not plan to stay for ever.

Pharaoh is generous. He gives them the best land and even offers them jobs over his own herds. A family of starving herders from Canaan now works for the king of Egypt.

Goshen is usually placed in the eastern Nile delta, though its exact borders are not known. It was good grazing land, and it lay on the side of Egypt nearest to Canaan.
passages.later: Israel never forgot that they began as guests in another land. When they brought their first harvest to God, they were to say, “My father was a wandering Aramean, and he went down to Egypt few in number and lived there and became a great nation, mighty and numerous” (Deuteronomy 26:5).
passages.asks: Pharaoh welcomed a family of hungry strangers and gave them the best of his land. Ask how you treat people who arrive in your town, your church or your workplace as outsiders. Then ask what Egypt's welcome might teach God's people about their own.

passages.happening:
“Then Joseph brought in his father Jacob and presented him before Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh” (verse 7).

“How many years have you lived?” Pharaoh asks (verse 8).

“My travels have lasted 130 years,” Jacob replies. “My years have been few and hard, and they have not matched the years of the travels of my fathers” (verse 9).

“Then Jacob blessed Pharaoh and departed from his presence” (verse 10). Joseph settles his family in the best part of Egypt, “the district of Rameses” (verse 11), and gives them food (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Picture the scene. The king of Egypt on his throne. Before him, an old herder from Canaan who owns no land at all. And the old man blesses the king, twice.

In that world, blessing usually flowed from the greater to the lesser. But this is the man God promised to bless, so that ‘all the families of the earth’ would be blessed through his family (12:3; 28:14). Here, in a small way, it begins.

‘My travels’ translates a word for living as a foreigner, a sojourner: someone who stays in a land that is not his own. That is how Abraham, Isaac and Jacob lived. Jacob sums up his life that way.

And he is honest. ‘Few and hard.’ Abraham lived to 175 (25:7), Isaac to 180 (35:28). Jacob's own years held the hatred of a brother, years of service to Laban, the loss of Rachel, the attack on Dinah and twenty years of grief for Joseph. He does not pretend.

‘The district of Rameses’ is a name from a later time. The city of Rameses was built by King Ramesses II in the 1200s BC, in the eastern delta. Many readers think Genesis uses the name its readers knew for the area. Others take such names as signs that the book was written down later. The book page on Genesis sets out the question of dates.
passages.later:
Hebrews says of Abraham's family, “they acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth” (Hebrews 11:13). A psalm prays, “I am a foreigner dwelling with You, a stranger like all my fathers” (Psalm 39:12).

Paul says the Scripture “foretold the gospel to Abraham: ‘All nations will be blessed through you’” (Galatians 3:8).
passages.asks: Jacob told the king the truth: his life had been short and hard. Ask whether you feel you must make your life sound better than it was, to God or to others. Then notice that the man who said ‘few and hard’ still had a blessing to give.

passages.t: Money, livestock, and at last themselves
passages.happening:
The famine grows worse in Egypt and Canaan (verse 13). Joseph collects all the money in both lands in exchange for grain, and brings it into Pharaoh's palace (verse 14).

When the money is gone, the Egyptians come to Joseph: “Give us food. Why should we die before your eyes? For our funds have run out!” (verse 15). Joseph tells them to bring their livestock. For a year he gives them food “in exchange for all their livestock” (verse 17).

The next year they come again. “There is nothing left for our lord except our bodies and our land” (verse 18). “Purchase us and our land in exchange for food. Then we, along with our land, will be slaves to Pharaoh. Give us seed that we may live and not die” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 41 told how Joseph stored the grain in the good years. This chapter tells what happened when the famine went on.

It is told in three steps. First the people pay with their money. Then with their livestock: horses, flocks, herds and donkeys. Last, with their land and their own bodies. Each time, the people come to Joseph because they are hungry.

The grain they are buying came from Egypt's own fields in the good years. Joseph had advised taking a fifth of the harvest (41:34), and he gathered the extra food and stored it in the cities (41:48).

The offer in verse 19 comes from the people themselves. ‘Purchase us and our land.’ They would rather be slaves than die. And they ask for seed, so that the land will not be left empty.

The narrator tells all this calmly. He does not praise it and he does not condemn it.
passages.later: Later Scripture knows how famine and debt can push people into bondage. In Nehemiah's day the poor cried out, “we are powerless to redeem them because our fields and vineyards belong to others” (Nehemiah 5:5). Proverbs says, “The people will curse the hoarder of grain, but blessing will crown the one who sells it” (Proverbs 11:26).
passages.asks: Starving people gave up their money, their animals, and at last their land and their freedom, to live. Ask what desperate people in your own world are forced to give up to survive. Then ask whether you have ever been on the side that gained from someone else's need.

passages.t: ‘Servants of Pharaoh’, and a fifth for ever
passages.happening:
“So Joseph acquired for Pharaoh all the land in Egypt” (verse 20). “And Joseph reduced the people to servitude from one end of Egypt to the other” (verse 21). Only the priests keep their land, because Pharaoh gives them rations (verse 22).

Joseph gives the people seed (verse 23). “At harvest time, you are to give a fifth of it to Pharaoh, and four-fifths will be yours as seed for the field and food for yourselves and your households and children” (verse 24).

“You have saved our lives,” they said. “We have found favor in our lord's eyes, and we will be Pharaoh's servants” (verse 25).

“So Joseph established a law that a fifth of the produce belongs to Pharaoh, and it is in effect in the land of Egypt to this day” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Say it plainly. By the end of the famine, the people of Egypt no longer own their land. Pharaoh does. The people farm it as his servants, and a fifth of every harvest goes to him, for good. Joseph built this, and he built it for Pharaoh.

There is a question about the words of verse 21. The usual Hebrew text says Joseph ‘moved the people to the cities’. The Samaritan copy of the first five books and the old Greek translation say he made them slaves. In Hebrew the two words differ by one letter. The Berean Standard Bible follows the second reading.

‘To this day’ shows the narrator writing at a later time, explaining a law his readers knew.

How should a reader judge what Joseph did? The narrator does not say. Readers answer in different ways, and the note on the hard verse below sets out the main ones. These notes take no side.
passages.later:
The story does not end here. Generations later a new king rose over Egypt. “So the Egyptians appointed taskmasters over the Israelites to oppress them with forced labor. As a result, they built Pithom and Rameses as store cities for Pharaoh” (Exodus 1:11). Then “The Israelites groaned and cried out under their burden of slavery” (Exodus 2:23).

Israel's own law, given after the exodus, says, “The land must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine” (Leviticus 25:23). An Israelite who sells himself because he is poor must not be made a slave, but released in the Year of Jubilee (Leviticus 25:39-41).
passages.hard:
Joseph's famine policy is one of the hardest parts of his story, and these notes will not soften it.

What the text says: the people sold their livestock, then their land, then themselves. Joseph made them servants of Pharaoh and fixed a fifth of every harvest as Pharaoh's share, for good.

Readers weigh it in three main ways.

Some read it as wise rule in a disaster. Joseph saved a nation from starving, and the people say so themselves: “You have saved our lives” (verse 25). They kept four-fifths of their harvest and were given seed.

Some add that the terms were mild by the measures of that world. The Laws of Hammurabi, from Babylon, speak of fields let out for half or a third of the harvest. Next to that, they say, a fifth was not a heavy share.

Others read the chapter more critically. Joseph used the people's hunger to gather all the money, animals and land of Egypt into the king's hands, and made free farmers into the king's servants. They point out that Israel's own law later forbade selling land for ever and making a poor Israelite a slave (Leviticus 25). And they notice where the story goes: the power Joseph built up for Pharaoh is the same throne under which Israel will be enslaved (Exodus 1).

The narrator does not comment, and these notes take no side. A reader can honor Joseph for saving lives and still see that Scripture does not hold up every policy of a faithful man as a model.

The site's Honest Answer, ‘Why didn't the Bible just ban slavery?’, faces the wider question of slavery in the Bible honestly and at length.
passages.asks: Joseph saved a nation and also made it Pharaoh's servant, and the Bible does not tell us what to think of it. Ask whether you can hold both truths about a person you admire. Then ask where, when you hold power over people in need, you may be tempted to take more than you should.

passages.happening:
“Now the Israelites settled in the land of Egypt, in the region of Goshen. They acquired property there and became fruitful and increased greatly in number” (verse 27).

Jacob lives in Egypt seventeen years and dies at 147 (verse 28).

When his death draws near, he calls Joseph. “Put your hand under my thigh and promise to show me kindness and faithfulness. Do not bury me in Egypt” (verse 29). “Carry me out of Egypt and bury me with them,” he says of his fathers (verse 30).

Joseph promises. “‘Swear to me,’ Jacob said. So Joseph swore to him, and Israel bowed in worship at the head of his bed” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
Notice the contrast with the passage before. The Egyptians lose their land. Israel gains property in Goshen and grows. God's promise to make Jacob a great nation (46:3) is already coming true.

Jacob came to Egypt at 130 and lives seventeen more years. Joseph was seventeen when his father lost him (37:2). Now Jacob has seventeen years with him at the end.

‘Put your hand under my thigh’ is an old way of making a solemn promise. Abraham's servant swore this way when he went to find a wife for Isaac (24:2). It touched the source of a man's family line, and so bound the promise to the family's future.

‘Kindness and faithfulness’ are two great Hebrew words, chesed and emet. Chesed is loyal love, the love that keeps its promises. Emet is truth, faithfulness, being someone who can be relied on.

Why not be buried in Egypt? Because Egypt is not the land God promised. Jacob wants to lie in the cave of Machpelah, which Abraham bought, with Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah (49:29-31). Even in death, Jacob points to the promise. His body will say what he believes: this family belongs in Canaan. (See the note on 12:4-9 for what the land promise means.)
passages.later:
Hebrews remembers Jacob's last days as an act of faith: “By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of Joseph's sons and worshiped as he leaned on the top of his staff” (Hebrews 11:21).

Exodus shows the promise of growth kept: “the Israelites were fruitful and increased rapidly; they multiplied and became exceedingly numerous” (Exodus 1:7).
passages.asks: Jacob lived in comfort in Egypt and still asked to be buried in the land of promise. Ask where your comfort has made you forget what you are waiting for. Then ask what choices you could make now that say where you truly belong.
